title: Process Priority
body:
A number in the [[PCB]] saying how badly this [[Processes|process]] wants the CPU. It is
the input to [[CPU Scheduling]]: given several processes in the [[Ready Queue]], run the
highest-priority one first.

Two sources for the number:

- **Static**: assigned when the process is created and never changes. Kernel threads and
  real-time tasks get high static priority.
- **Dynamic**: the scheduler adjusts it as the process runs. A process that keeps blocking
  on I/O gets boosted (it is not a CPU hog and it wants short bursts), a process that burns
  its whole time slice gets lowered.

Implementation is usually one [[Ready Queue]] per priority level rather than one queue that
gets sorted. Pick the front of the highest non-empty queue; within a level it is plain
[[FIFO]] round robin.

## Why priority alone is not a scheduler

Strict priority is unfair by construction: if high-priority processes keep arriving, a
low-priority one never runs. That is [[Starvation]], and it is the reason
[[Bounded Waiting]] is one of the three requirements rather than a nice-to-have. The fix is
**aging**: raise a process's priority the longer it has been waiting, so anything in the
ready queue eventually reaches the top. Aging is what turns priority into something with a
bound on waiting time, and it is the trade against [[Fairness]].
